overview.headline: From layered rocks to atomic clocks, how geologic time was revealed

keyPoints.point: Earth has a vast time span that people find hard to grasp.
keyPoints.quote: Earth is 4.54 billion years old, a span of time that is hard for many people to grasp.

keyPoints.point: Superposition places older rocks on the bottom and younger rocks on the top in layered strata.
keyPoints.quote: The law of superposition says that older rocks are on the bottom and younger rocks are on the top.

keyPoints.point: Uniformitarianism says modern Earth processes also shaped Earth in the past and future.
keyPoints.quote: states that the processes that we see happening on Earth today are the same processes that shaped Earth in the past

keyPoints.point: Half-life decay to stable daughter isotope lets scientists measure absolute rock age from parent remainder.
keyPoints.quote: A half-life is the length of time it takes for half of the number of original, or parent, isotopes to decay to a stable daughter isotope.

keyTerms.gloss: Older layers lie below younger layers in undisturbed sedimentary order.
keyTerms.quote: The law of superposition says that older rocks are on the bottom and younger rocks are on the top.

keyTerms.gloss: Principle that past geologic change used same processes seen today.
keyTerms.quote: In 1788, James Hutton proposed what would become the foundational principle of geology — uniformitarianism.

keyTerms.gloss: Distinct fossil species groups mark the same age wherever they appear in order.
keyTerms.quote: Smith developed the law of faunal succession, which states that species become extinct and are replaced by new species

keyTerms.gloss: Time for half the parent isotopes to decay to daughter product.
keyTerms.quote: A half-life is the length of time it takes for half of the number of original, or parent, isotopes to decay to a stable daughter isotope.
